description: Hi! I'm a ICT/engineering student with a genuine love for space and science — this is my first NASA Space Apps Challenge and I'm excited to build something real, not just talk about it. I'm working on the Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts challenge: a dashboard that tracks simulated astronaut vitals (cardio, bone/muscle, radiation, sleep) and flags issues early. Looking for teammates of any skill level.
summary: VITALS is a crew-health monitoring prototype that helps astronauts recognize changes in simulated health telemetry during long-duration missions. It compares readings such as heart rate, HRV, SpO₂, sleep, temperature, and exercise against a personal 30-day baseline. Deterministic detection rules flag unusual readings and multi-signal deviations, while the console presents the exact measurements and rules behind each alert in plain language. NASA research metadata provides scientific context. By making changes easier to spot and alerts easier to understand, VITALS supports timely crew awareness while clearly distinguishing evidence from diagnosis. All demonstration data is simulated; the prototype is not a medical device.
details:
VITALS replays simulated crew-health telemetry through a browser-based console. It compares each reading with the preceding 30 readings to build a personal baseline, then applies deterministic rules to flag readings that deviate by at least two standard deviations. A 48-hour rule highlights cases where two or more signals deviate across the latest daily readings. Each alert shows the measurements, baseline statistics, z-scores, and rule that triggered it, helping crew understand what changed rather than presenting an unexplained warning.

The goal is to support crew awareness and timely review during long missions, where access to medical support may be limited. The team prioritized personal trends, transparent evidence, and careful wording: alerts are not diagnoses or treatment advice, and all demo data is simulated. NASA Open Science Data Repository study metadata provides context, not diagnostic conclusions.

The project uses Python with FastAPI and WebSockets for the replay and backend, and HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the interface. It runs in a standard web browser and requires no specialized hardware. Its creative approach combines personalized baselines, multi-signal detection, and evidence-first explanations in one crew-facing console.
